claims.text: The alloy is a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with distinctly segregated phases.
Under inert or low-oxygen conditions, the alloy forms minimal continuous oxide scale.
Increasing ambient oxygen potential during elevated-temperature wear-corrosion testing promotes oxide-film formation relative to an inert atmosphere.
An oxygen-rich high-temperature environment causes oxides to form preferentially at interphase boundaries.
The interphase-boundary oxide films are brittle and non-adherent.
Distinct phases in the alloy have different oxidation kinetics at elevated temperature.
Differential oxidation kinetics produce mechanically weak oxides at phase boundaries.
Simultaneous wear repeatedly spalls the interphase-boundary oxides.
Repeated oxide spallation exposes fresh metal surfaces.
The exposed fresh surfaces undergo accelerated localized corrosion through galvanic coupling between disparate phases.
Relative to an inert-atmosphere baseline, the oxygen-rich condition will produce higher total degradation.
Relative to the baseline, the oxygen-rich condition will increase the wear rate because of frequent oxide spallation.
Relative to the baseline, the oxygen-rich condition will increase the corrosion rate because of intensified galvanic attack.
The controlled comparison uses identical alloy samples tested under otherwise identical elevated-temperature wear-corrosion conditions in oxygen-rich and inert atmospheres.
The proposed mechanism is limited to multi-phase eutectic HEAs with distinctly segregated phases under controlled elevated-temperature wear-corrosion conditions.
Failure of the oxygen-rich condition to show higher wear, higher corrosion, and interphase-boundary oxide spallation relative to the inert control would falsify the proposed mechanism.
